channel.title: OAM reference: contributor notes :: Go Kure — Launcher
channel.description: Each page here belongs to one part of the OAM and component reference (api-reference/oam and api-reference/oam-components). It holds what a contributor needs and a reader of the reference does not: the code that implements an entry, the issues behind it, and the tests that hold its claims. A page is named after its reference part and has one section per entry, with up to three lists: Implementation: the helper or file that builds the entry. History: the issues that introduced or changed it. Tests: the tests that hold a claim of the reference, with the claim each one holds. Text on these pages is moved from the reference without rewording. A claim stays in the reference; its test or issue reference moves here.

item.title: Policy defaults, endpoints and outputs
item.description: Implementation, history and tests of the sections on the reference page Policy defaults, endpoints and outputs. Text in square brackets is added here to say what a moved sentence refers to. Policy defaults & enforcement ordering Implementation: enforce.go’s applyDefaultQuantity [“fills any request/limit the author left unset”, in the reference’s tier 2.] oam.PolicyDefaultReporter: the workload kinds, cnpg-cluster, persistentvolumeclaim and the pvc trait embed an oam.PolicyDefaultLog; the scaler trait implements the interface itself, so that its config stays comparable [“is reported to the provenance report as a policy entry”, in the reference’s tier 2.] oam.BuiltinDefaultReporter, embedded oam.BuiltinDefaultLog in cnpg-cluster [“is reported as a builtin entry”, in the reference’s tier 2.] common.go ["buildResourceRequirements", in the reference’s tier 3.] capPolicyRequestDefaults, resource_policy_defaults.go [“held to the authored limit for that resource”, in the reference’s tier 3.] enforceMaxResources (enforce.go) closes this by calling the same buildResourceRequirements the generator calls, enforcing against its result, and discarding it — buildResourceRequirements deep-copies its maps, so this is read-only and generated output is unchanged. [“this” is the gap described in the History entry below it.] cnpgResourceList [“copies every entry of c.Resources straight onto the Cluster spec”, in the reference’s sentence on postgresql.] common.go’s buildResourceRequirements call sites at the init-container and sidecar builders [“receive the same intrinsic defaults”, in the reference’s paragraph on init containers and sidecars.] enforce.go [“the shared enforceExtraContainer helper”, in the same paragraph.] common.go [“a dedicated JobSpecConfig/parseJobSpec/applyJobSpec”, in the reference’s paragraph on the twelve JobSpec-level properties.] applyJobSpec copies every value it writes rather than assigning the config’s own pointers (copyPtr for the scalars, DeepCopy for successPolicy and podFailurePolicy, which each own a slice of rules). A handler config outlives one Generate call and Generate may run more than once, so an aliased pointer would leave a mutable path from the generated object back into the config — a writer through the object would change what the next Generate emits. History: go-kure/launcher#1181 [“an authored opt-out”, in the reference’s tier 1.] go-kure/launcher#1217; the apiserver refuses a request above its limit [“renders a 64Mi request, not 128Mi”, in the reference’s tier 3.] Prior to go-kure/launcher#251 the enforcement check ran before the intrinsic tier was computed, so an application that omitted spec.resources entirely could ship a Deployment whose 100m CPU / 128Mi memory intrinsic defaults exceeded the enforced maximum. [“the enforcement check” is the check of oam.Policy.MaxCPU()/MaxMemory() described in the reference’s paragraph on the effective value.] go-kure/launcher#312 ["ApplyPolicy enforces them too", in the reference’s paragraph on init containers and sidecars.] go-kure/launcher#344 ["job onto its own spec", in the reference’s paragraph on the twelve JobSpec-level properties.] Tests: Both halves are pinned: TestSchemaJobSpec_HasNoSuspendKey on the schema, TestCronjobHandler_SuspendWritesCronJobSpecOnly and TestJobHandler_SuspendWritesJobSpec on the generated objects. [“Both halves” are the two halves described in the reference’s paragraph “One JobSpec field is deliberately not shared: suspend”.] Policy refusal classes Implementation: enforce.go, enforcePodTemplatePolicy, enforceRenderedObjectPolicy [“one check raises it”, in the reference’s first bullet.] History: go-kure/launcher#849 [“instead of matching text”, in the reference’s first paragraph.] Pod view of a monitoring workload object (MonitoringPodSpec) History: go-kure/launcher#974 [“finds none to scan”, in the reference’s first paragraph.] Tests: Each monitoring workload kind adds its case from its own monitoringWorkload mapping; TestMonitoringPodSpec_CoversEveryRegisteredWorkloadKind (pkg/oam/builtin/registry) fails on a registered kind of the operator’s API whose spec lists containers and that has no case. [“its own monitoringWorkload mapping” is also “the same mapping” in the reference’s bullet “What it holds”.] Declared endpoints of a chart Implementation: chartEndpoints [“One shared schema and parser”, in the reference’s first paragraph.] History: go-kure/launcher#1132 [“implement oam.EndpointProvider from an endpoints property”, in the reference’s first paragraph.] Tests: the schema-parity test names endpoints as its one exception ["helmrelease decodes the rest as its HelmReleaseSpec", in the reference’s bullet “Not a chart value”.] Declared outputs History: go-kure/launcher#1259 [“implement oam.OutputProvider”, in the reference’s first paragraph.]

(“the whole list” is the reference’s “Required” list, the 59 fields and the two more it names, and “one” is a field of that list; the test is in cilium_clusterwidenetworkpolicy_internal_test.go.) (“Each” is each of the five kinds, gatewayclass, gateway, listenerset, referencegrant and backendtlspolicy, “that one object” is the Gateway API object the kind is the projection of, and “the storageclass entry” is on the reference page Kinds: core workloads.) item.title: Kinds: Flux
item.description: Implementation, history and tests of the entries on the reference page Kinds: Flux. Every test named here is in pkg/oam/builtin/components/flux_kinds_internal_test.go unless a line says another file. fluxcd-alert, fluxcd-provider, fluxcd-receiver, imagepolicy, imagerepository, imageupdateautomation, artifactgenerator, resourcesetinputprovider Implementation: Each is built on policyFreeKind (see the storageclass entry) with the Flux namespace, the check of its durations and, where a field names a host the environment policy holds or holds a credential, a check under that policy (fluxKind), and emits that one object, named after the component unless objectName names it; the handler adds no label, no annotation and no default. (“the storageclass entry” is on the reference page Kinds: core workloads.) History: go-kure/launcher#790 (the kind-named projections). go-kure/launcher#601 (a duration is held to the pattern its field declares). go-kure/launcher#619 (a timeout of an hour or more is written in minutes, as the timeout of a Flux source is). go-kure/launcher#984 (a Receiver resource’s apiVersion is checked at build time). go-kure/launcher#1010 (the version the refusal names for a kind outside the Receiver API’s kind enum). go-kure/launcher#883 (the Required lists are generated from the markers of the Go source, and the CRDs are vendored for the tests). go-kure/launcher#874 (a kind checks an expression rule only where the check is held to the API server’s own validator, which answers from a CRD). go-kure/launcher#975 (a pagerduty Provider’s routing key in channel). go-kure/launcher#1079 (a trait in a later group that makes a required read is refused). Tests: TestFluxKinds_DefaultedZeros holds each kind’s list of such fields to the numbers, booleans and strings that are omitted when zero and that the API defaults to something else. (“such fields” are the reference’s fields that the type omits when empty and the API defaults, as eventSeverity and filter.limit.) TestFluxKinds_MarkersClassified fails on a field the type writes unauthored that neither a marker nor that rule classifies. (“that rule” is the reference’s “schema generators’ rule” for a field with no marker whose json tag keeps it when empty.) A dependency bump that adds, drops or moves one fails there. (“there” is TestFluxKinds_MarkersClassified, and “one” is a field the type writes unauthored that a marker or that rule classifies.) A null survives as a null rather than becoming an empty {}/[]. item.title: The null contract and two spellings of one field
item.description: Implementation, history and tests of the sections on the reference page The null contract and two spellings of one field. Text in square brackets is added here to say what a moved sentence refers to. The null contract Implementation: authoredValue — the presence primitive parseStringField, parseObjectField, parseInt32Field, parseInt64Field, parseObjectList and parseStringList all go through — does exactly that, so calling any of them directly already complies. They classify a typed nil as null too — map[string]any(nil) or []any(nil) inside an any, which is what a lowering rule assembled in Go produces for an unset optional and is not == nil. [“that” is the reference’s “read a null under an optional property as omission”; “They” are the six helpers named in this sentence.] A new optional field is read with the helper for its type instead: parseStringField (or requiredStringField when the field is required), parseBoolField, parseInt32Field, parseInt64Field, parseObjectField, parseObjectList or parseStringList. Each already reads an explicit null as absence through authoredValue, so a wrapper would only repeat that check. [“instead” is instead of an optional* wrapper; “a wrapper” is one of those, listed under History.] History: It is written down because “null” has several readers — the emission validator’s requiredness check and its optional-key strip, its array-element guard, enforcePlatformReserved, this package’s parsers, and the Kubernetes API itself — and each was aligned separately, so each round of review found the reader the last round had not touched. [“It” is the reference’s rule on the null contract.] This used to require a separate optional* wrapper family (optionalString, optionalObject, optionalInt32, optionalInt64, optionalObjectList, optionalStringList) layered in front of the plain parsers. go-kure/launcher#394 moved the handling into the shared helpers themselves, which made every wrapper an exact no-op forward; they were removed and every caller now uses the parse* helper directly. go-kure/launcher#423, go-kure/launcher#394 and go-kure/launcher#570 converted the parsers they covered; the last of them are listed with the null row of the deployment table above. [“the parsers they covered” are the parsers that answer presence with a bare v, ok := props[key], the first limit of the reference; “the deployment table above” is on the reference page of the deployment kind.] Both limits met on one key, and it was the second row of that table. namespaceSelector is parsed twice in this repository: here, for pod affinity, through parseSchedulingSelector (parseObjectField), where any null is omission — which upstream reads as “this pod’s namespace”; and in the networkpolicy trait, through parseNPPeer. A typed nil used to satisfy the networkpolicy trait’s own type assertion and yield an empty selector — all namespaces, the widest possible answer — while an untyped nil already read as omission there, so one input landed on opposite ends of the range depending on which Go nil shape produced it. Both parsers now route their presence check through oam.IsNullValue’s reflect-based classification, which treats a typed nil the same as an untyped one, so the two halves converge: a null namespaceSelector, however it was constructed, is omission on both paths. [“Both limits” are the two limits the reference lists; “that table” is its labelSelector and namespaceSelector table; “here” is the handler parsers.] The same typed-nil shape reached list elements. parseObjectList read a null key as absence, but a typed-nil element ([]any{map[string]any(nil)}) passed its per-element assertion as an empty object, where an untyped null element is refused (tolerations[0]: must be an object, got <nil>).
